posts.title: 🚨FQL TODAY. BELDEX NEXT? STOP. THINK. VERIFY.
posts.author: Sreekar Aadhini Balaji

🚨FQL TODAY. BELDEX NEXT? STOP. THINK. VERIFY.

What if the biggest crypto mistake isn’t buying at the wrong price?

What if you trusted the wrong platform?

FQL is already a warning.

Reports allege that FQL attracted investors with extraordinary return promises, including claims of doubling money within 40-45 days. Authorities investigated the matter, with arrests reported.

But here’s the question:

Would you trust a crypto platform simply because it has a website, a token, a community and thousands of followers?

Look at BELDEX.

This is NOT a claim that Beldex has been legally established as a scam.

But recent events deserve serious attention before anyone puts money into BDX.

⚠️BDX-BSC BRIDGE INCIDENT

Beldex reported unauthorized minting of approximately 38.2 million BDX-BSC tokens through an issue in its bridge infrastructure. The affected bridge was paused, followed by remediation and migration measures.

⚠️INCORRECT MASTERNODE REWARD

Beldex reported that approximately 900 million BDX was incorrectly generated instead of the expected 6.25 BDX reward.

The response included Hardfork 21 and a rollback of around 1,327 blocks.

⚠️TOKEN MIGRATION

Kraken announced the migration from legacy BDX to a new BELDEX token, with the legacy token scheduled for delisting and withdrawals only.

Now stop and ask:

Would you investigate these events or simply trust a promoter saying BDX is the “next big opportunity”?

🚨THAT IS THE WARNING.

A website ≠ safety.

A token listing ≠ credibility.

A Telegram community ≠ proof.

A successful withdrawal ≠ investment security.

A promised return ≠ a proven business model.

Before investing:

🔍VERIFY the legal entity.

📊UNDERSTAND where the returns come from.

🔐CHECK who controls the infrastructure.

📄READ incident reports, not just promotional posts.

💰NEVER send money for “guaranteed” returns.

🚫NEVER connect your wallet through an unsolicited link.

👥NEVER invest simply because an influencer, friend or referral agent says you should.

FQL is a warning about trusting promises.

Beldex is a reminder to examine technology, security and infrastructure risk.

The lesson is simple:

DON’T INVEST BECAUSE SOMEONE SAYS, “TRUST ME.”

Verify independently.

Understand the risks.

Then decide.

Because in crypto, your money can move in seconds, but recovering it may take much longer.

🚨FQL TODAY.
BELDEX TODAY.
YOUR DUE DILIGENCE MUST COME FIRST.

THINK BEFORE YOU INVEST.

Remember before clicking BUY:

⚠️Visibility is not credibility.
⚠️A functioning app is not proof of safety.
⚠️FOMO is not due diligence.
⚠️One successful withdrawal does not prove an investment is safe.

When a platform faces a security incident, token migration, ask:

What happened?
Who controls the response?
What changed?
How were users protected?
What risks remain?

posts.title: This is the 4th fake recruiter I’ve encountered in the past 2 months. And this one was much better executed than the usual scams.
posts.author: Ron Ng.
posts.snippet:
This is the 4th fake recruiter I’ve encountered in the past 2 months. And this one was much better executed than the usual scams.

The approach looked completely normal.

A recruiter contacted me on LinkedIn about a senior APAC role at Anchorage Digital, quoting a $270k-$330k package, remote work and equity.

We exchanged a few messages. No pressure. No strange questions. No request for passwords, personal documents or money.

They proposed a call, asked for my email and sent a meeting invitation. Everything moved at the pace of a normal recruitment conversation.

The trap only appears once you join the meeting (I suspected so I used a complete brand new browser profile to join just to test out).

During the video call setup, there is supposedly a "problem connecting your camera" (it's fake). Then, you are then given a command to paste into Terminal to “fix the issue".

That command is the payload. Run it and you may effectively be installing malware on your own computer, potentially giving the attacker access to your device, credentials, wallets and other sensitive information.

I spotted it before running anything, so nothing happened. But this is now the 4th recruiter account or recruitment approach I’ve encountered in roughly 2 months that turned out to be compromised or fraudulent.

That frequency is getting ridiculous.

A few things worth remembering, especially for people working in crypto, fintech and Web3:

- A legitimate recruiter should never need you to run a Terminal, PowerShell or command-line command to join an interview.
- A polished LinkedIn profile means very little if the account itself has been compromised.
- A realistic salary, professional writing and a slow conversation are no longer signs that the approach is legitimate.
- If video or audio “doesn’t work”, leave the meeting and use another platform. Never install their fix.
- If someone sends you a command, script, browser extension or executable during recruitment, assume it is hostile until independently verified.

The newest scammed account is Arhum Younas , so others can be careful around them. As with previous scam accounts, they blocked me right away once the invitation was sent or they realised that their scam technique had been spotted. The accounts themselves may also have been compromised, so I’m describing what happened rather than making assumptions about who is actually behind them.

Please share this with anyone currently job hunting in crypto or tech. The scams are getting quieter, slower and much more convincing.
posts.reason: Ron Ng describes sophisticated recruitment scams targeting crypto/fintech workers with malware payloads—directly relevant to CISOs, compliance officers and law enforcement investigating fraud infrastructure that Bloctopus investigates.

comments.text: The terminal-command trick is notable because it shifts the compromise from credential phishing to direct device access, which means the attacker isn't just after passwords but potentially wallet files and session tokens sitting locally on the machine.

Did the meeting invite come from a domain that at least superficially resembled Anchorage's own, or was it a generic scheduling tool - that detail matters a lot for how these campaigns are being built at scale.

We've traced funds from cases that started exactly this way, a convincing recruitment conversation followed by a device compromise, and by the time the victim noticed anything wrong the wallets had already been drained and layered across chains within the hour.

posts.title: Ever had a deployment succeed, verified that the files are present in your storage bucket, and still ended up staring at a 404 Not Found?
posts.author: Tushar Seth
posts.snippet:
Ever had a deployment succeed, verified that the files are present in your storage bucket, and still ended up staring at a 404 Not Found?

I recently ran into this while deploying a frontend update on Google Cloud.
The CI/CD pipeline completed successfully, and the newly generated .js and .css files were present in the Cloud Storage bucket.

But the live application was still returning 404s for those assets.

After tracing the request flow, the issue turned out to be negative caching at the CDN layer.
A previous request had returned a 404, and that response had been cached. So even after the asset was successfully uploaded to the origin, subsequent requests could still receive the cached 404 instead of reaching the storage bucket.

The important lesson: a successful deployment doesn't necessarily mean the latest version is being served.

When debugging similar issues, it's worth checking the complete delivery path:
Browser → CDN → Load Balancer → Origin
and looking at:
Cache status
Negative caching configuration
TTLs
Cache-Control headers
CDN invalidation

Understanding what happens between your deployment and the end user can make these issues much easier to diagnose.

Sometimes the code is deployed correctly.
It's the cache that's still serving yesterday's answer. 

Have you encountered a similar CDN caching issue during a deployment?

posts.snippet:
Fraud is evolving — and due diligence must evolve with it.

A recent OCCRP investigation highlights a crypto fraud network allegedly targeting victims across the EU through fake investment platforms, social engineering and digital deception.

The bigger takeaway for organisations is clear:

Due diligence cannot stop at documents and databases.

Understanding who is behind the information and independently corroborating it is becoming increasingly important in identifying hidden risks.

At Trudicon, we believe effective due diligence combines document verification, identity checks, field intelligence and independent corroboration to build a more complete risk picture.

Verify beyond the paperwork. Identify the risk.

#Trudicon #DueDiligence #FraudPrevention #RiskManagement #BackgroundVerification #FinancialCrime #DigitalFraud
posts.reason: Abhishek Kohli discusses crypto fraud networks and evolving due-diligence methods—highly relevant to compliance officers, exchanges and forensic teams in Bloctopus's target audience.

comments.text: Document and database checks tell you what a counterparty claims to be; they say nothing about how the funds actually move once they enter a wallet or platform. Fake investment platforms in particular tend to hold up fine on paperwork but collapse the moment you trace the fund flow behind them.
In your field intelligence work on cases like this, how often does the corroboration step actually surface a link back to a previously known fraud network, versus flagging something entirely new?
We regularly get engaged after the documents already looked clean - the fraud only becomes visible once you follow where deposited funds were swapped, bridged or consolidated on-chain.

posts.title: US Treasury wants banks to be better at filing cyber scam reports after noting nearly $13 billion in losses since 2023
posts.author: Technology Matters
posts.snippet:
US Treasury wants banks to be better at filing cyber scam reports after noting nearly $13 billion in losses since 2023  

The US Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network has issuespublished an alert and a companion data analysis telling banks, credit unions, digital asset exchanges, and securities firms that it needs sharper reporting on the overseas scam centers that it says target Americans at an industrial scale.FinCEN puts total damages, per its reporting mechanism, at roughly $12.7 billion linked to suspected digital asset investment scams between September 2023 and the end of 2025.The number comes from adding up the dollar values of 33,904 Bank Secrecy Act filings that referenced the keyword from its 2023 "pig butchering" alert, which may be overstated, as it includes both attempted and successful transactions as well as both inbound and outbound reports, often of the same transactions, causing significant overlap.FinCEN's new requirement is a keywordWhile the $12.7 billion is a measure of what institutions have flagged and is prone to double-counting and errors, victim losses, a significant chunk of which go unreported, may be considerably higher.This has prompted Gene Lange, who effectively works as the Under Secretary for Terrorism and Financial Intelligence, to call these scams "one of the most significant fraud threats facing Americans today."It has also prompted a new suspicious activity report keyword: "FIN-2026-SCAMCENTERS," which institutions are expected to use to indicate that a scam center is potentially involved.FinCEN also wants chat logs, scammer phone numbers, social media handles, wallet addresses, transaction hashes, and the URLs victims were told to deposit into, filed in the structured cyber indicator fields rather than left out.Institutions to volunteer more information to stop scamsThe move is part of its push to have institutions volunteer more information under the US Patriot Act, as it aims to confront what is a growing intelligence problem: scammers tend to route victims through several institutions in sequence; most filers see only one slice of a scam's lifecycle and often have difficulty tracing it all the way.For example, a crypto exchange might see a customer buying USDT and sending it off-platform, a bank might see a wire to that exchange, and a brokerage might see a retirement account liquidated. None of them would have the bigger picture of what essentially happened or what triggered the transaction.Combined, with properly linked information, it makes it much easier to identify a potential scam; separately, these incidents can inflate the number of reports, which often aren't linked, and investigations can lack insight into the origin or final destination of the funds.FinCEN's Rapid Response Program has interdicted $1.8 billion and recovered just over $1 billion for 5,790 US victims since 2015, which, against the flagged totals, is a very limited recovery at best compared with the actual funds at stake. This highlights a larger fundamental problem: institutions mostly detect these schemes after the money is gone, and reporting them correctly and thoroughly may yield limited dividends at best against an industry that has morphed, relatively unchecked, into a multi-billion-dollar juggernaut.  

https://lnkd.in/d7dXXvUJ
posts.reason: The US Treasury/FinCEN alert on investment-scam reporting requirements and crypto asset tracking directly addresses AML, compliance and law-enforcement audiences central to Bloctopus's mission.

comments.text: The double-counting problem FinCEN flags is real, but even a conservative reading of 33,904 filings shows institutions are now systematically capturing something they mostly missed two years ago. The bigger gap is still the unreported victim losses, which structured SAR fields alone won't close.

Will requiring wallet addresses and transaction hashes in structured fields actually change how quickly institutions escalate to blockchain analytics, or will it just improve after-the-fact statistics without speeding up real-time response?

We've seen how much easier a case becomes when the initial report already includes wallet addresses and tx hashes rather than a narrative description - it can be the difference between tracing funds before they're layered across chains and starting from scratch weeks later.

posts.title: What a day.
posts.author: Chad Adolph
posts.snippet:
What a day.

As today’s CI-FIRST Financial Crime Forum comes to a close, I’m incredibly thankful for everyone who gave their time, experience, and perspective to make the day meaningful.

I had the privilege of moderating two very different conversations.

This morning’s Law Enforcement and DOJ Regional Financial Crime Threat Briefing brought together leaders from the FBI, Homeland Security Investigations, IRS Criminal Investigation, and the U.S. Attorney’s Office to discuss the evolving threat environment, major fraud threats, money-mule networks, transnational financial crime, and the importance of connecting pieces of financial intelligence that no single organization can see alone.

This afternoon, I moderated Protecting the Financial System Together with retired DEA Supervisor Timothy Reagan, now with Chainalysis, and IRS-CI Special Agent Rich Gourley, one of our agency’s leading cryptocurrency investigators.

We discussed the growing intersection between traditional finance and digital assets, what blockchain analytics can reveal, how investigators follow money across both systems, and why financial institutions and law enforcement increasingly need to understand both. Rich then brought those concepts to life through a case study showing how traditional financial records, digital-asset tracing, and investigative tools work together.

I’m also grateful to U.S. Attorney Dominick Gerace for delivering the keynote and emphasizing the national-security importance of tackling fraud with urgency and coordination.

Our financial-institution partners added critical private-sector perspective on fraud trends, AML challenges, emerging typologies, and where stronger collaboration is needed.

Supervisory Special Agent Kevin Doyle also did what he does so well — showing how following the money, tracing transactions, and patiently putting the pieces together can dismantle major drug-trafficking organizations when other investigative efforts have stalled.

IRS-CI ASAC Kyle Brice, CFE moderated the Ohio Fraud Model with IRS-CI Daniel Cobb Assistant US Attorney Ryan Saunders, Ohio AG Office Gregory Haines discussing proactive partnerships and approaches to combatting fraud.

Thank you as well to our Treasury partners from OFAC, FinCEN, and IRS Civil Exam/BSA Compliance for sharing their expertise.

One theme came up again and again:

No single agency, financial institution, regulator, prosecutor, or technology platform sees the entire picture.

The advantage comes when we connect the pieces.

Better information sharing. Better feedback. Better relationships. Fewer silos.

Very grateful to Lauren Kohr , Jennifer Sturdivant the CI-FIRST team, Jonathan Buffington and Kroger as well as every panelist, speaker, and attendee who contributed.

After more than 26 years in federal law enforcement and now entering the final chapter of public service, days like today are a meaningful reminder of why these partnerships matter.
posts.reason: Chad Adolph reports on the FBI, IRS-CI, DEA and financial institutions collaborating on blockchain analytics and cross-border money-tracing—core to Bloctopus's law-enforcement and AML buyer segment.

comments.text: The point about connecting pieces no single organization can see alone is the crux of most crypto-linked financial crime cases - the on-chain trail and the traditional banking trail each tell half a story, and neither agency typically owns both halves.

In the case study Rich walked through, was the initial lead generated from the traditional financial records or from the blockchain side, and did that origin point change how the rest of the investigation was sequenced?

Combining digital-asset tracing with traditional financial records is exactly where we spend most of our time on cross-border cases - the crypto leg gets you the flow, but the fiat leg is usually what makes it prosecutable.

We had valuable conversations with banking and financial services leaders about the evolving financial crime landscape and the opportunities to modernise compliance through technology.

A key highlight of the day was Bryan Scott K.'s panel discussion, "From Accounts to Assets: How Fraud Proceeds Are Layered and Structured," where he explored emerging money laundering typologies, beneficial ownership transparency, and the growing complexity of tracing illicit funds across digital assets and corporate structures.

Thank you to everyone who shared their perspectives with us. We look forward to continuing the conversations and partnering with financial institutions across Malaysia on their compliance transformation journeys.

posts.title: One more crypto exchange is shutting down this year, and the reason reveals a troubling reality about the economics of running an exchange.
posts.author: Nitin Gupta
posts.snippet:
One more crypto exchange is shutting down this year, and the reason reveals a troubling reality about the economics of running an exchange.

CoinEx Global announced on September 15 that it will wind down after 9 years, with operations ending on December 22.

The exchange says reserves remain above 100%, has published proof of reserves, and is giving users roughly three months to withdraw. Remaining CET will be bought back at its original $0.005 listing price.

I’ve been watching crypto infrastructure closely, and CoinEx is not alone. BitMEX, BitMart, AscendEX, and CoinEx have all announced shutdowns or orderly wind-downs in 2026.

The economics are getting harder for mid-sized exchanges.

CoinEx ranked around 33rd by trading volume, with roughly $58 million in daily volume against $174 million in assets.

More importantly, TRM Labs traced more than $3.84 billion in flows between CoinEx and sanctioned Iranian entities.

That makes founder haipo yang’s comment particularly relevant... “Carrying unlimited risk for limited revenue is no longer a rational choice.”

The pressure is structural. Trading volume concentrates around deeper-liquidity venues. Compliance costs remain significant regardless of scale. And a single sanctions, security, or fraud issue can create liabilities far beyond the revenue generated by a customer.

That gap isn't market conditions. It's whether customer assets were actually there all along. A wind-down is simply when everyone finds out.

I think crypto is consolidating into a handful of deep-liquidity venues plus specialised regional players with real licences. The middle disappears.

The surviving advantage stops being token listings, it becomes provable solvency, clean flows, and jurisdictions you can actually operate in.

If your exchange closed tomorrow, would you get your money back?

posts.reason: Nitin Gupta's detailed analysis of exchange consolidation, sanctions compliance, and solvency—including specific mention of TRM Labs tracing $3.84B in Iranian flows—is directly relevant to compliance officers, regulators, and lawyers evaluating exchange risk and AML/source-of-funds verification.

comments.text: Proof of reserves is necessary but not sufficient - it tells you assets exist at a snapshot, not whether flows to sanctioned counterparties like the $3.84bn TRM identified were ever properly screened. Solvency and clean flow history are two different questions.
With a three-month withdrawal window, how many users actually move funds out promptly versus assuming it's someone else's problem until the deadline is near?

We've traced funds through exchanges mid-wind-down before, and the practical issue is rarely reserves - it's that support and compliance staff are already gone by the time users start asking questions, which slows any dispute resolution to a crawl.

posts.title: We Used to Draw the Map Before We Built the Road
posts.author: Matthew Curnow
posts.snippet:
We Used to Draw the Map Before We Built the Road

Who remembers the whiteboards?

Not so long ago every process optimisation and automation project I worked on started the same way: a room full of sticky notes, a facilitator asking, "walk me through what actually happens," and hours spent tracing the As-Is process, every handoff, every exception, every workaround someone had invented. We'd redesign the To-Be state, and then automate the workflow.Somewhere in the last two years, that discipline quietly disappeared.

I have seen a move to a new pattern: PoC First, Process Never
Working in organisations today I see a different rhythm. Someone initiates an AI proof of concept and it gets a demo and applause. Then it stalls and never quite makes it into the actual workflow. 

The old operating model challenge - does it need to change? 
The old data science model was fundamentally a project structure, not a process structure. A team would get a narrow, well-bounded question, prediction, demand forecasting, build a model, hand over an API or a dashboard, and move to the next backlog item. The unit of work was the model, not the process it sat inside. That's partly why it never needed deep BPM-style collaboration: the scope was narrow enough that "redesign the whole workflow around this" was rarely necessary.

GenAI and contextual/domain AI break that assumption in two ways.

The unit of work is no longer a model, it's a workflow. 
A classic example here is predictive maintenance: feed in sensor data, output a failure-probability score, drop it into a field on the asset register. One model, one number, one handoff. An contextual Agentic solution for asset maintenance doesn't work that way, it reads the failure score alongside the equipment manual, past work orders, and parts inventory, then drafts the work order, flags who should be dispatched, and checks whether the part needs ordering. That's not a prediction in a field anymore; it's participating end to end in a process spanning the reliability engineer, the planner, the technician, and procurement. 

Skip the workflow redesign, and all you get is some accurate PoC models. 

From experience the data backs up 
Most organisations know that to achieve the outcomes using GenAI PoC's the people and the workflows must change, yet what we see it that AI teams typically dont fund the work to redesign the processes and skills needed to change. 

The results achieved through the enablement of cross function collaboration teams, where we have GenAI skills working hand in hand alongside our industry and domain specialists,  turning a clever demos into the future workflows.....we are capturing the incentive changes that AI implies. 

If you would like to learn more about how we are designing for the AI future please feel free to reach out to me.

posts.title: 24 hours. That’s Revolut’s deadline.
posts.author: WEB3 Newswire
posts.snippet:
24 hours. That’s Revolut’s deadline.
A group calling itself “iamnotavillain” is demanding 6,000 Monero, worth around $3 million.

Pay up, they say, or the stolen customer data goes to other criminal groups.

At least 680 Revolut accounts were reportedly affected.

Passports. Driving licences. 
KYC photos. Transaction histories.

But the part that stands out is how the targets were allegedly chosen.

They weren’t random.

The hackers told the Financial Times they used blockchain analysis to identify Revolut accounts holding significant crypto.

So your crypto activity may not just reveal what you own.
It could help someone decide whether you’re worth targeting.

And the breach didn't require some sophisticated attack on Revolut's infrastructure.

It reportedly started with social engineering.

The attackers posed as government officials and sent requests that passed Revolut’s internal checks. 

Staff then handed over genuine customer records before the fraud was discovered.

Revolut says customer funds weren't affected and that law enforcement was notified.

But the data is another story.
And there's a reason the ransom is being demanded in Monero.

XMR is designed to make transactions significantly harder to trace than those on Bitcoin or Ethereum.

At the time of the FT report, no negotiations had started.

The bigger question is uncomfortable:
What happens when your on-chain activity can help identify you as a high-value target?

#Revolut #CryptoSecurity #Monero #Web3 #DataBreach
posts.reason: The Revolut breach post combines blockchain analysis targeting, social engineering, ransomware extortion in Monero, and data theft—directly illustrating the intersection of crypto tracing, forensics, and incident response that Bloctopus specializes in, with clear relevance to compliance, law enforcement, and CISOs.

comments.text: Using on-chain analysis to pick targets by wallet balance is a meaningful escalation - it means holding visible crypto wealth now carries a social-engineering risk that has nothing to do with how secure your own wallet is. The exposure sits with the custodian's data, not your keys.

Given the ransom is in Monero specifically to resist tracing, does law enforcement have any real leverage here beyond the usual choke-point pressure on the exchanges the ransom eventually has to touch to become spendable?

We've seen this pattern before with insider-assisted verification bypasses: the weak point is almost never the blockchain, it's a human approving a request that looks procedurally correct on the surface.

posts.author: Jay. Adil
posts.snippet:
The KPK’s seizure of Rp106.3bn and detention of eight suspects in the Summarecon land case is not merely another graft scandal. It shows how corruption in Indonesia has become embedded: land permits, HGB extensions and court disputes are treated as rent-seeking opportunities. A Rp2bn demand negotiated down to Rp1.5bn captures the normalization public authority priced, bargained and sold.

Key points:
· Scale: cash in red suitcases at former Kebumen Regent Arif Sugianto’s home: Rp31.86bn, $2.61m, S$1.97m, plus riyals/ringgit; Rp896m at businessman Rizal Pahlevi.

🚩 Recruitment layered on investing, If the pitch spends more time on "bring your friends" than the actual strategy, that's a red flag for a pyramid structure, not a fund.

- Verify the person or firm through your country's regulator (e.g., SEC/FINRA BrokerCheck in the US, FCA Register in the UK).
- Ask what license they hold and check it directly with the regulator, not via a link they send you.
- Be skeptical of any advice tied to urgency, secrecy, or upfront payment.
- Remember: real financial professionals rarely need to DM strangers for clients.

Protecting your capital starts with protecting yourself from bad actors who are counting on you not to check.

One more crypto exchange is shutting down this year, and the reason reveals a troubling reality about the economics of running an exchange.

The exchange says reserves remain above 100%, has published proof of reserves, and is giving users roughly three months to withdraw. Remaining CET will be bought back at its original $0.005 listing price.

I’ve been watching crypto infrastructure closely, and CoinEx is not alone. BitMEX, BitMart, AscendEX, and CoinEx have all announced shutdowns or orderly wind-downs in 2026.

The economics are getting harder for mid-sized exchanges.

CoinEx ranked around 33rd by trading volume, with roughly $58 million in daily volume against $174 million in assets.

More importantly, TRM Labs traced more than $3.84 billion in flows between CoinEx and sanctioned Iranian entities.

That makes founder haipo yang’s comment particularly relevant... “Carrying unlimited risk for limited revenue is no longer a rational choice.”

The pressure is structural. 

Trading volume concentrates around deeper-liquidity venues. Compliance costs remain significant regardless of scale. And a single sanctions, security, or fraud issue can create liabilities far beyond the revenue generated by a customer.

That gap isn't market conditions. It's whether customer assets were actually there all along. A wind-down is simply when everyone finds out.

I think crypto is consolidating into a handful of deep-liquidity venues plus specialised regional players with real licences. The middle disappears.

The surviving advantage stops being token listings, it becomes provable solvency, clean flows, and jurisdictions you can actually operate in.

If your exchange closed tomorrow, would you get your money back?

He asked a simple question:
"We have DLP, encryption, access controls and monitoring. But if a sensitive document is copied, shared, modified or passed into an AI tool, how do we trace its journey?"
That question deserves more attention than it gets.
Because data security is not only about preventing unauthorised access. It is also about knowing where your data travels, who touches it, and what happens to it afterwards.
This is where data watermarking becomes important.
A watermark can embed identifiable information into a document, image, dataset, report or other data asset. Depending on the technology, it can help establish ownership, identify the source, detect unauthorised redistribution, and support forensic investigation.
Think of it as giving your data a traceable identity.
Now consider the AI era.
Data is moving into AI assistants, enterprise copilots, analytics platforms, third-party applications, model-training pipelines and external collaboration environments.
The challenge is no longer just:
"Who accessed the data?"
It is also:
"Where did the data go next?"
"Was it copied, transformed, shared or used somewhere else?"
"Can we trace its origin if it appears outside the intended boundary?"
Watermarking, combined with DLP, encryption, access governance, data lineage, audit logs and AI governance, can strengthen that visibility.
It is not a replacement for security controls. It is an additional layer of accountability.
As the Operational CEO of Candid Brains, I believe organisations must move from “protecting data at rest” to “protecting and tracing data in motion, in use and across AI ecosystems.”

- Vishing calls where someone pretends to be IT support or a bank to get you to reveal credentials
- Fake "security alerts" pushing you to click or verify credentials
- Requests that create pressure to act fast, before you can think it through

A few habits that help:
1. Slow down. Urgency is a tactic, not a reason to skip verification.
2. Verify through a separate channel. Call the company directly using a number you already know, not one from the email or text.
3. Question unexpected requests for personal or account info, even ones that look official.

Security isn't just your risk and compliance team's job. It's a habit built one cautious pause at a time.

Revolut is a global fintech with 80M+ customers and banking licenses in jurisdictions around the World. In September it confirmed sensitive customer data was disclosed after receiving fraudulent information requests sent from a legitimate government agency email domain.

Identity and contact details (name, DOB, addresses, phone, email), copies of passports/driver’s licences, and potentially verification selfies, account statements, and full transaction histories—including crypto. Lots of useful information for identity theft, account takeover, targeted phishing, and financial fraud. For high‑net‑worth users, it also supports extortion and sophisticated social engineering.

Why would the bank disclose such information?

One of the best methods of identifying and tracking criminals is to "follow the money." Financial institutions are legally obliged to respond to lawful government and law‑enforcement requests in support of investigations, sanctions, tax, money laundering, etc. A "digital supply chain service" provided to law enforcement and government agencies. As with all supply chains, security is only as strong as the weakest link. If you can't get through the bank's security, maybe you can compromise the government systems?

What could be done better?

It appears Revolut trusted the governmental email domain as sufficient authentication and provided the information requested. In other words, they were phished.
Dealing with the money side of banking, we leverage multi-factor authentication. Secondary authentication controls like, phone calls, code phrases, passkeys -- any number of ways to validate the request. Perhaps the risk assessment for "information" from a bank didn't identify the need for stronger authentication.

Trust is a fundamental element of all systems. It is especially important when the system involves multiple parties. You have to trust that a request from the other party is legitimate. If you aren't sure, ask for additional proof of authenticity until you have established trust. And never trust email. It is a complicated, poorly understood and poorly secure system. Ripe for compromise.

Revolut: Stolen Customer Data Is Already Being Used for Blackmail

We previously covered the Revolut data breach, in which attackers obtained sensitive customer information through fraudulent requests impersonating a government agency. New details have now emerged about how the attack worked and what happened to the stolen data afterward.

According to Kela, the fraudulent emails were sent through a compromised government agency account and successfully passed SPF, DKIM, and DMARC checks. Revolut’s compliance and legal teams treated the requests as legitimate and manually provided the requested files.

According to sources cited by GovInfoSecurity, the attacker gained access to a system used by Italian federal employees. The initial compromise is believed to have involved a remote access trojan (RAT). The attacker then reportedly spent several months testing different social engineering scenarios. Eventually, a compromised government email account and a European Investigation Order were used to request customer data from Revolut.

The Financial Times estimates that approximately 680 customers were affected. Screenshots published by a person using the alias IAmNotAVillain showed a 326 MB folder containing 688 files. Crypto investigator ZachXBT reported that the targets included wealthy cryptocurrency holders. Former Mt. Gox CEO Mark Karpelès and crypto entrepreneur Marc Zeller were among those who publicly confirmed receiving breach notifications.

The consequences began before Revolut officially disclosed the incident. Gamdom founder Felix Römer said that he and other victims had received extortion demands roughly two months before the breach became public. As evidence, he published a screenshot of a blackmail attempt dated July 26.

From a security perspective, the most significant part of this case is the attack chain itself. Compromising a single trusted government account gave the attacker a way to turn a legitimate data disclosure process into an exfiltration channel. Email authentication worked as intended, the request appeared official, and the data left the company through employees who were legitimately authorized to access it.

The case illustrates an important boundary between email security and business process security: SPF, DKIM, and DMARC can verify where an email came from, but they cannot verify whether the request inside it is legitimate. Operations involving sensitive data therefore need separate authorization controls and independent verification before a request is fulfilled.

posts.title: When an RFI Becomes a Data Breach: The Revolut Case from a Compliance Perspective
posts.author: Rogério Nzita
posts.snippet:
When an RFI Becomes a Data Breach: The Revolut Case from a Compliance Perspective

Revolut recently confirmed that confidential customer information was disclosed to an unauthorised third party after the company received fraudulent Requests for Information.

According to Reuters, the Financial Times and TechCrunch, the requests were submitted through an email address associated with a legitimate government agency domain. By impersonating public officials, the individuals behind the scheme convinced Revolut that the requests were genuine.

The incident reportedly affected approximately 680 customers. The information potentially disclosed included contact details, residential addresses, identity documents, verification photographs, bank statements and transaction histories.

Although Revolut stated that its core infrastructure, customer accounts and funds were not compromised, the incident reveals a significant Compliance and data-protection risk.

A legitimate email domain does not necessarily prove that the person using it is authorised. Before responding to an RFI, financial institutions should:

• Independently verify the requester’s identity and authority;
• Confirm the request through a separate official channel;
• Validate the case reference, jurisdiction and legal basis;
• Apply four-eyes approval before disclosing sensitive information;
• Share only the information strictly necessary;
• Monitor repeated, unusual or high-risk requests.

The case is particularly concerning because some affected customers reportedly held significant crypto assets. Combining residential addresses, identity documents and financial information can facilitate identity theft, targeted phishing, extortion and even physical threats.

The key lesson is clear: Compliance is not simply about responding to a request that appears official. It is about questioning, authenticating, limiting and documenting every disclosure.

Criminals do not always need to hack a bank’s systems. Sometimes, compromising a trusted communication channel and persuading an institution to disclose information is enough.

Trust without independent verification can become a vulnerability.

posts.author: GND Cyber

Your recovery plan may be answering a question nobody asked.

Some extortion campaigns no longer encrypt anything. Data is taken quietly and the demand arrives afterwards. No locked screens, no halted production, no obvious moment when the incident announces itself.

That removes the trigger most response plans are built around. Backups, rebuild speed and immutable storage all assume something stopped working. When nothing did, the clock that matters is a disclosure clock, and it started before anyone knew.

Detection has to rest on something else. Access patterns that do not match the role. Data moving between systems with no reason to exchange it. Volume leaving the environment that nobody scheduled.

Open your incident playbook. Which step comes first, restoring or notifying?

posts.author: Nicklesh Madoori

AgenticSecOps - Module 4: Vulnerability Prioritization & Patch Agent

Most vulnerability scanners produce a list nobody reads. Hundreds of CVEs, sorted by a CVSS score that doesn't tell you what's actually being exploited in the wild versus what's theoretical.

The one that matters gets lost in the noise - and that's usually the one that turns into a ransomware event.

The VPP agent: 

→ Trivy or Grype (both free, OSS) do the actual scanning - containers, dependencies, the usual sources.
→ The agent cross-references every finding against CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog - a free, continuously updated feed of what's actually being used in real attacks right now, not just theoretically severe.
→ Everything gets ranked: patch now, patch this sprint, or monitor. Only "patch now" means known-exploited AND sitting on a critical or internet-facing asset.
→ Draft PRs get opened for low-risk, high-confidence fixes only. A human still approves every patch window - auto-merging security patches without a staging test is how you trade a vulnerability for an outage.

The gap this closes: the average ransomware payout is running around $2M, on top of downtime that costs roughly $53K/hour. Most of that is preventable by patching the handful of CVEs that were already known to be exploited before the breach happened.

posts.title: The most useful ransomware statistic I've read this year isn't about ransom amounts. It's about how attacks start.
posts.author: Ron Klink
posts.snippet:
The most useful ransomware statistic I've read this year isn't about ransom amounts. It's about how attacks start.

79% of ransomware attacks began with an identity-based approach. Not a zero-day. Not an exotic exploit. Somebody logged in.

Sophos surveyed 2,158 IT and security leaders across 17 countries, all at organizations that had been hit in the previous twelve months. The root causes: malicious email 26%, phishing 24%, compromised credentials 23%, exploited vulnerabilities 18%, brute force 6%. Add up the first three and you get the shape of the problem — the front door, opened with a real key.

This changes what "security" should mean in a small business. Most of what gets sold is designed to keep strangers out of the building. But if the attacker is arriving with valid credentials, the firewall watches them walk in and holds the door.

What actually moves the needle — about 45 minutes:

1. Multifactor on every account, no exceptions, especially the ones nobody uses. The service account, the shared mailbox, the old admin login. Exceptions are where this fails.
2. Reduce the number of people with admin rights to the number who genuinely need them today, not the number who needed them in 2022.
3. Separate daily work from admin work. Nobody should read email from an account that can change your tenant.
4. Turn on sign-in alerts for impossible travel and unfamiliar locations, and decide who reads them. An alert nobody reads is decoration.
5. Review who still has access from the last three people who left. This is where I find something almost every time.

Here's the part worth sitting with: only 34% of organizations with 100 to 250 employees stopped an attack before their data was encrypted. At organizations of 3,000 to 5,000, it was 46%. Smaller companies aren't attacked more cleverly. They're attacked the same way, with less time to notice.

posts.title: Reading a blockchain ledger is straightforward. Tracing stolen cryptocurrency across it is not.
posts.author: Pinnacle Blocks
posts.snippet:
Reading a blockchain ledger is straightforward. Tracing stolen cryptocurrency across it is not.

The distinction matters because it shapes what investigators actually do and what the output of that work needs to be. The public, permanent nature of blockchain transactions is a genuine forensic advantage. Every transfer is recorded. No institution needs to be compelled to produce it. But the existence of the record and the ability to follow it purposefully are different capabilities, and confusing them produces strategies that look credible until they encounter the methods serious thieves actually use.

A thief moving funds across a single wallet to a single exchange is an edge case. What investigators more commonly encounter is a deliberate layering process. Funds split across multiple addresses. Deposits into mixing services that pool inputs and redistribute outputs in ways designed to interrupt simple transaction following. Chain-hopping, where assets are bridged from one blockchain to another specifically because the analytical tools tracking them on the first chain do not automatically extend to the second. Each of these techniques adds a layer that requires methodological work to penetrate, not just ledger access.

The forensic process that handles this complexity operates on several levels simultaneously. Address clustering identifies wallets that, despite appearing independent, exhibit behavioural patterns consistent with shared control. Transaction timing analysis finds correlations between deposit and withdrawal events that survive mixing. Exchange deposit identification locates the points where layered funds eventually reach regulated infrastructure, because those points are where compliance obligations attach and where legal intervention becomes actionable. None of that is automated. It is analytical, requiring judgment about what the data pattern means and how that interpretation would survive adversarial scrutiny.

That last phrase carries real weight. Locating funds on a blockchain is not the same as building a chain of evidence that holds up in court. The forensic record that supports a freezing application, a proprietary tracing order or an expert report tendered in civil proceedings has to withstand challenge. The methodology needs to be documented. The reasoning at each hop needs to be defensible. The connection between a theft wallet and an exchange deposit address several steps removed has to be established through traceable analytical steps, not asserted.

Every hop a thief takes does leave a trail. But reading that trail accurately, and translating it into something a court will act on, is the work. The ledger is where the work starts. It is not where the work ends.

A trace that stops at 'funds entered a mixer' is analytically interesting but operationally useless; the report only earns its keep once it lands on a regulated on-ramp or off-ramp with a compliance obligation attached.

When timing correlation survives mixing but clustering evidence is circumstantial, how do you present that confidence gap in a report meant to withstand adversarial scrutiny - as a probability range, or do you simply flag it as unresolved?

We've had cases where chain-hopping was clearly deliberate, the thief picked the second chain specifically because the analytics coverage there was thinner, and closing that gap required manually rebuilding clustering heuristics that just didn't exist yet for that network.

posts.title: This article highlights a critical operational reality: financial institutions often gain their clearest visibility only when a payment is being executed, while the earliest preven
posts.author: Thieu Nguyen Bao Chau, CIA CAMS
posts.snippet:
This article highlights a critical operational reality: financial institutions often gain their clearest visibility only when a payment is being executed, while the earliest prevention signals may already exist elsewhere.

The fraud lifecycle typically involves four stages:
1. Recruitment and relationship building through social media, messaging platforms, dating apps, and other digital channels.
2. Manipulation and conversion, including the promotion of fraudulent investment platforms and the use of small “test” transactions.
3. Payment execution, where funds move through banks, fintechs, payment apps, or crypto exchanges.
4. Laundering and cashout, involving mule accounts, crypto wallets, cross-chain transfers, mixers, OTC brokers, and offshore services.

=> Key lesson is clear: effective fraud prevention depends on connecting data across sectors and acting at the right time.
High-value signals include:
- Social-media account clusters, reused identities, scam scripts, wallet addresses, and advertising identifiers.
- Email authentication failures, lookalike domains, forged headers, and suspicious wire instructions.
- SIM-swap events, number-porting activity, short phone-number tenure, and VoIP indicators.
- Newly registered domains, reused SSL certificates, fast-flux DNS, and hosting churn.
- Micro-entry activity, beneficiary mismatches, rapid payment-rail switching, remote-desktop usage, and unusual device behavior.
- Crypto wallet clusters, transaction hops, mixer or bridge interactions, chain switching, and incomplete Travel Rule information.
Structured victim narratives that connect the digital, behavioral, and financial elements of a scam.

A more resilient anti-fraud ecosystem should therefore focus on:
Mapping which organization holds each critical data element.
Establishing trusted and legally sound information-sharing channels.
Prioritizing real-time or near-real-time signals.
Sharing durable network intelligence rather than isolated indicators.
Treating victim reports as structured intelligence.
Measuring success through prevented losses, faster intervention, effective takedowns, and improved recovery.

Fraudsters understand the ecosystem better than many defenders do. Closing the gaps requires financial institutions, technology companies, telecom providers, crypto platforms, fraud consortia, regulators, and law enforcement to build a shared view of the fraud lifecycle—and act together before funds disappear.

posts.title: Crypto VC funding is back. Crypto VC Rose 31%. Early-Stage Companies Received Just 22% of It.
posts.author: Thomas van der Linde

Crypto VC funding is back. Crypto VC Rose 31%. Early-Stage Companies Received Just 22% of It.
Crypto venture funding reached $5.68 billion in Q2 2026, according to Galaxy Research. That sounds like a broad recovery. The underlying numbers tell a much narrower story.

Investment increased 31% from Q1, but the number of deals rose only 10%, from 355 to 384. The median deal reached a quarterly record of approximately $4.9 million. The reason is concentration. Later-stage companies captured 78% of all capital invested. Early-stage businesses shared the remaining 22%, even though pre-seed rounds alone represented 21% of completed transactions.

One sector dominated the quarter. Trading, exchanges, investing and lending companies raised $3.52 billion—62% of all crypto venture funding. More than 90% of the capital invested in this category went to later-stage businesses.

The geographic divide was equally stark. US companies completed 39.1% of the deals but captured 73.5% of the capital. The UK received 4%, while France took 3.2%.

Fundraising showed the same pattern. Just five new crypto-focused funds raised approximately $3.9 billion—the fewest funds launched in a quarter since 2019.

And despite the Q2 rebound, the first half of 2026 produced $10.02 billion across 744 deals. At that pace, the year would finish at approximately $20.04 billion—still marginally below the $20.3 billion invested in 2025.

This is not another indiscriminate crypto funding boom. More capital is being controlled by fewer funds, deployed through larger rounds and concentrated in later-stage US companies operating around trading, lending and financial infrastructure.

Crypto VC is growing again. But for early-stage founders outside the US, the market may actually be getting harder. Source: Galaxy Research, Q2 2026. Original reporting by Olivia Stephanie.

Each one has its own name, its own on-chain track record, its own capacity ceiling, its own follower base, and its own performance share. They are three separate, independently investable products.

etoro is the opposite: one Popular Investor runs one portfolio. You copy the person. If they make bad calls in crypto while you only wanted their equity picks, you're along for the ride anyway.

120 people. 131 independently verified, independently tracked, independently investable products. And that ratio grows as analysts build confidence and expand across sports and markets.

The model is the credential. The on-chain track record is the proof. The analyst is the person who built both, and who can build as many as their edge allows.
 
That's not a tipster platform. That's a verified intelligence marketplace.

posts.title: The 2026 Revolut Breach Proves One Thing: A Convincing Email is Now More Dangerous Than a Zero-Day Exploit. 🚨
posts.author: David C.
posts.snippet:
The 2026 Revolut Breach Proves One Thing: A Convincing Email is Now More Dangerous Than a Zero-Day Exploit. 🚨
Recently, Revolut suffered a massive data breach affecting high-net-worth clients. Passports, biometric selfies, and crypto transaction histories were all handed directly to extortionists. But here is the terrifying part: Revolut wasn't hacked.  
There was no malware on their servers. No brute-force attacks. Instead, cybercriminals executed a flawless Law Enforcement Email Compromise (LEEC). Using infostealer logs bought on the dark web, attackers hijacked a legitimate government email domain. Because the emails passed SPF, DKIM, and DMARC checks, compliance teams trusted the domain and manually fulfilled the fabricated "official" data requests.  
This incident exposes a massive blind spot in the financial sector: We have hardened our IT perimeters, but we leave our legal and compliance intake processes shockingly vulnerable to social engineering.
Under APRA's Prudential Standard CPS 230 and the Australian Privacy Act 1988, this type of systemic failure isn't just an embarrassment; it’s a direct regulatory violation. Failing to secure sensitive personal information against social engineering can now result in penalties of up to $50 million, or 30% of adjusted turnover, in Australia, alongside severe actions under the New Zealand Privacy Act 2020. Relying on human intuition to spot fake Emergency Data Requests (EDRs) is no longer a viable strategy.
So, how do we fix this? We must enforce Zero Trust for Legal Requests, and it requires the right technology.
If an integrated resilience platform like Noggin (by Motorola Solutions) had been utilized, this breach could have been systematically prevented:
🔒 Mandatory Out-of-Band Verification: Noggin’s workflow engine can be configured to halt any data release until a compliance officer formally logs a phone call to the agency's official, publicly listed number.
🛑 Automated Checklists & Dual Authorization: The system removes human error by forcing rigid, un-skippable validation steps before sensitive KYC data can be exported.
⏱️ CPS 230 & Privacy Compliance on Autopilot: If a breach does occur, Noggin automatically triggers strict 24-hour and 72-hour APRA reporting playbooks, pre-filling regulatory templates (including OAIC/NZ Notifiable Data Breaches) and alerting stakeholders instantly.
Authentication is not verification. Just because an email comes from a legitimate .gov.au or .govt.nz domain does not mean the person typing it is a police officer. It’s time we arm our compliance teams with the same level of automated, zero-trust technology that we give our SOC analysts.
How is your organization verifying law enforcement data requests? Are you trusting the domain, or are you verifying the human? Let’s discuss below. 👇

posts.title: Red Flags in Cash Transactions – AML/KYC
posts.author: Institute of AML & Financial Compliance
posts.snippet:
Red Flags in Cash Transactions – AML/KYC

Cash transactions are not automatically suspicious. But when cash activity is unusual, inconsistent, or difficult to explain, it can become an important AML red flag.

🔎 Key red flags AML/KYC analysts should watch for:
1️⃣ Large cash deposits – Unusually high cash activity compared with the customer profile.
2️⃣ Multiple small deposits – Repeated smaller transactions that may indicate structuring.
3️⃣ Frequent cash transactions – Regular deposits or withdrawals without a clear economic purpose.
4️⃣ Third-party deposits – Cash deposited by individuals who have no obvious relationship with the account holder.
5️⃣ Activity inconsistent with the profile – Cash volumes that don't match the customer's occupation, income, or expected activity.
6️⃣ Round-number transactions – Repeated deposits or withdrawals in unusual round amounts.
7️⃣ Cash-intensive businesses – Cash activity significantly higher than what would reasonably be expected for the business.
8️⃣ Frequent cash withdrawals – Repeated withdrawals, particularly when followed by rapid movement of funds.
9️⃣ Geographic concerns – Cash activity involving locations associated with elevated financial-crime risk.
🔟 Rapid movement after cash deposits – Funds quickly transferred to other accounts, third parties, or overseas.

💡 Important: A single red flag does not automatically mean money laundering. Analysts should consider the overall customer profile, transaction history, source of funds, purpose of the activity, and supporting evidence.

📌 AML analysts should ask:
👉 Is the activity consistent with the customer's profile?
👉 Is there a reasonable economic purpose?
👉 Can the source of funds be reasonably explained?
👉 Are there multiple red flags occurring together?

Spot the pattern. Investigate the activity. Document your findings.

The Land Office registers thirty years. A promise of two more terms, the "30+30+30", is a contract with your current landlord, not a registered right. If the land is sold, inherited or the company folds, that promise can go with it.

By default the lease also ends when the lessee dies. Hold it through a corporate lessee and it does not.

The Thai company route is closing fast: source-of-funds proof since January, sworn declarations since April, 21 agencies enforcing. The amendment that would make nominee shareholding a money-laundering offence is not law yet, but the direction is set.

posts.title: A Rs 25,938 crore incentive is announced for clean mobility. None of it is cash until a factory clears one test. That gap, between an announcement and a payout, is worth understand
posts.author: Technofunda Research
posts.snippet:
A Rs 25,938 crore incentive is announced for clean mobility. None of it is cash until a factory clears one test. That gap, between an announcement and a payout, is worth understanding.

PLI Auto puts about Rs 25,938 crore over five years behind incremental sales of advanced automotive technology, battery-electric and hydrogen vehicles and their components. The incentive is sales-linked, roughly 13 to 18 percent for vehicle makers and 8 to 13 percent for component makers, on eligible incremental sales.

Start with the number people quote. The Rs 25,938 crore outlay is the ceiling the scheme can pay over five years. It says nothing about how much has actually reached a manufacturer's bank account. An approval, a budget line and a disbursal are three different numbers.

The money moves along a claim-to-cash cycle: R&D and tooling spend, then domestic sourcing, then an eligible sale, then domestic-value-addition verification, then an incentive claim, then cash. Cash sits at the far end, after the test and the audit.

That test is the gate. To earn a rupee, a maker must prove at least 50 percent domestic value addition on the eligible product, verified independently. Importing a kit and bolting it together is low domestic value and clears nothing; making the hard parts at home is high domestic value and qualifies. The incentive is a localisation test with cash attached.

And even after a sale qualifies, an accrual is not cash. The maker still has to decide when to book the incentive, at sale, at certification, at claim, at approval, or at cash receipt, and the gap between the sale and the cash is working capital it funds itself. So the incentive lifts economics over time, it is not a day-one margin boost.

The other side, fairly put. The incentive is real, and rising as more players clear the domestic-value test and scale eligible sales. It genuinely lowers the cost of building clean-mobility capacity at home. But an outlay is not a disbursal, only a fraction converts, the test and verification are slow, and an accrual is not cash.

So read any production-linked incentive by four questions. Is the number an outlay, a budget, or an actual disbursal? What is the eligibility test, here at least 50 percent domestic value addition? How long is the claim-to-cash cycle? And is the income booked at sale, or only at cash?

An incentive is a promise. Cash comes after the test. Watch the domestic-value-cleared disbursal, not the headline outlay.

posts.title: Indonesia’s evolving legal framework has introduced three public funding mechanisms for the protection and recovery of crime victims: the TPKS Law (Law No. 12 of 2022), the KUHAP (
posts.author: Indonesia Judicial Research Society (IJRS)
posts.snippet:
Indonesia’s evolving legal framework has introduced three public funding mechanisms for the protection and recovery of crime victims: the TPKS Law (Law No. 12 of 2022), the KUHAP (Law No. 20 of 2025), and the PSdK Law (Law No. 3 of 2026). These laws provide for restitution, compensation, and support for victim recovery services. However, despite their shared objective, significant differences remain in how each mechanism is regulated and implemented.

The three mechanisms can be understood as forming a tiered funding structure. The KUHAP Endowment Fund provides the overarching framework for financing compensation, rehabilitation, restitution, and related forms of redress. The PSdK Victim Assistance Fund (DAK) provides a dedicated allocation for compensation, restitution, and victim recovery programmes. The TPKS Victim Assistance Fund (DBK), meanwhile, operates as a more specific mechanism for providing benefits to victims of sexual violence crimes.

Against this backdrop, this policy paper examines the legal and institutional relationship among the three mechanisms. The analysis focuses on governance arrangements, the potential overlap of institutional mandates, accountability for funding and fund management, disbursement mechanisms, and institutional coordination and division of responsibilities. Clearer arrangements are essential to ensure that the availability of funding translates into accessible and effective recovery support for victims.

We recommend:
1. Harmonising the scope of offences eligible for victim recovery services across the three funding mechanisms.

2. Separating victim recovery financing from financing related to rights arising from errors in criminal justice administration.

3. Integrating the respective funding sources into a single, coordinated platform for victim recovery financing.

4. Establishing the Victim Endowment Fund under a two-key governance model, whereby the Ministry of Finance manages fiscal matters and LPSK determines eligibility, needs, forms and amounts of assistance, priorities, and service duration.

5. Clarifying the DAK disbursement and service-delivery mechanism, including whether victims may apply directly, whether access is based on LPSK needs assessments and programmes, and whether funding may be provided without awaiting a court decision, as under the DBK scheme.

Read more IJRS and
Lembaga Perlindungan Saksi dan Korban (Indonesia Witness and Victim Protection Agency) policy paper here: https://lnkd.in/gZ-HgBTb

FINANCIAL NEWS THAT MATTERS

Two SME IPOs opened for subscription today, September 17.

But the bigger lesson for promoters is not about the IPO.

It is about a question that every growing company eventually faces:
Should we fund the next stage of growth through debt or equity?

Consider a company that needs ₹50 Cr for expansion.

It could potentially choose:

Option 1 — Debt
Bank / NBFC / NCD / Private Credit
↓
No ownership dilution
↓
But interest + repayment obligations

Option 2 — Equity
Promoter contribution / strategic investor / IPO / private equity
↓
No fixed repayment obligation
↓
But potential dilution of ownership

So which one is better?

There is no universal answer.

The decision should depend on the company's:
Cash-flow visibility
Existing leverage
Profitability
Debt-servicing capacity
Asset base
Growth stage
Cost of capital
Promoter's willingness to dilute

Here's a simple way to think about it:

If the business has:
✅ Strong and predictable cash flows
✅ Healthy EBITDA
✅ Comfortable leverage
✅ Good debt-servicing capacity
Then debt may be a suitable source for funding expansion.

But if the company has:
⚠️ High leverage
⚠️ Uneven cash flows
⚠️ Large upcoming capex
⚠️ Long gestation period before cash generation

Then adding more debt may increase financial pressure, and equity or a combination of equity and debt may need to be considered.

And there is a third option:

Don't think only in terms of Debt vs Equity.
A company can build a funding mix.
For example:
₹50 Cr expansion
→ ₹15 Cr internal accruals
→ ₹20 Cr term debt
→ ₹10 Cr equipment finance
→ ₹5 Cr equity

The right combination depends on the company's financial position and the nature of the investment.

One question every promoter should ask:
“What should my balance sheet look like after I fund this growth?”

Not just:
“How much money can I raise?”

Because raising capital is only one part of the decision.
The real objective is to fund growth without putting unnecessary pressure on the balance sheet.

For companies planning expansion, refinancing or a significant funding requirement, comparing debt, equity and structured funding options before committing to one route can make a meaningful difference.
